article_content: After being released from prison in 2012, following four years served for marijuana-related charges, Frederick Hutson recognized an underserved market. Hutson then founded Pigeonly, a platform that allows incarcerated individuals to share photos and make low-cost phone calls, thereby helping 50,000 people maintain connections with their loved ones. Pigeonly's success story underscores the potential of technology created by and for underrepresented communities. The tech industry faces a significant diversity gap, as evidenced by the fact that 99% of venture capital-funded startups in 2010 were founded by whites or individuals of Asian descent, predominantly men. Reviving American capitalism requires making it more inclusive by investing in diverse talent and innovative ideas.

article_content: During Barack Obama's presidency, the US national debt rose by more than $7 trillion, from '$10.626 trillion' on January 20, 2009, to '$17.687 trillion' by July 31, 2014. This increase is notable as it took the first 43 presidents 223 years to accumulate the first '$7 trillion' in debt. Obama's debt increase was significantly higher than his predecessors, with George W. Bush adding '$2.720 trillion' and Bill Clinton adding '$1.324 trillion' after the same number of days in office. The Congressional Budget Office warned that the growing federal debt could restrain economic growth and increase the risk of a fiscal crisis.

article_content: Washington (CNN) -- Predictions of super PAC-fueled campaign ugliness came to reality on Thursday when reports broke of a potential conservative group's ad campaign aimed at tying President Barack Obama to a controversy many thought was put to rest nearly four years ago. But conservative billionaire Joe Ricketts decided against a recommendation from GOP strategists that would bring up once again Obama's association with the controversial Rev. Jeremiah Wright, a super PAC director said. Wright, who once ran the church that Obama attended in Chicago, became a central figure in the 2008 election when videos emerged showing some of the pastor's provocative statements involving race relations in the United States. Obama distanced himself from Wright to help spare his political image. The proposal to bring Wright back into campaign dialogue quickly became the story of the day. After hours of backlash from both Republicans and Democrats, Ricketts said the plan was one of several proposals his group was considering. Brian Baker, who heads the conservative super PAC supported by Ricketts, said Ricketts would not approve the scheme, as it 'reflects an approach to politics that Mr. Ricketts rejects.' 'Mr. Ricketts intends to work hard to help elect a president this fall who shares his commitment to economic responsibility, but his efforts will be focused entirely on questions of fiscal policy, not attacks that seek to divide us socially or culturally,' Baker said in a written statement.

article_content: By Ted Thornhill. The world's largest collection of vintage tennis posters, spanning a century, is up for sale for $170,000 at Swann Auction Galleries, known as 'the Wimbledon of auctions'. The posters, dating from the late 19th century, advertise various items including famous tennis tournaments, luxury destinations, and cars. A highlight is a 1930 poster by French artist Roger Broders advertising Monte Carlo. The collection includes posters with estimated values ranging from $250 to $20,000. Nicholas Lowry, president of Swann Auction Galleries, stated that the collection is the largest ever to come to auction and covers a century of tennis history.

article_content: The owner of a high-end vegetarian restaurant in London has been convicted of animal cruelty for neglecting a herd of cattle on his smallholding. Khalid Undre's 'Down to Earth' restaurant in Kensington High Street promoted itself as 'environmentally sound and animal friendly', but RSPCA inspectors found his cows were underfed, dehydrated, and left to suffer in harsh winter conditions. Undre was found guilty of failing to provide adequate food, water, and care for his Red Poll cattle, leading to the deaths of some animals. The RSPCA's investigation, prompted by a tip-off, revealed a stark contrast between Undre's business ethos and the reality on his farm.

article_content: Facebook announced on Monday that it's rolling out a new 'Replies' feature, allowing users to respond directly to comments on their page. This feature aims to make navigating conversation threads easier. Responses will be posted under the original comment. The site will prioritize comments based on engagement, surfacing the most active ones to the top of posts. The feature will initially be available on desktop and will be rolled out to pages with over 10,000 followers by July 10, 2013.

article_content: (CNN) -- The third body recovered in Yosemite National Park near where three hikers were swept over a waterfall in July has been identified as missing 21-year-old 'Ramina Badal', park officials said on Tuesday. The bodies of the other two hikers had previously been identified. In July, witnesses said the three -- two men and a woman -- climbed over the guardrail at the top of a trail and went into the gushing river that feeds the waterfall, known as 'Vernal Fall'. They were quickly swept over. Park officials had previously said that a body found by a park ranger on November 29 was determined to be that of 'Ninos Yacoub', 27, of 'Turlock, California'. His body was found in the 'Merced River' about half a mile below the base of the waterfall. Yacoub was with 'Hormiz David', 22, of 'Modesto, California', and Badal, of 'Manteca, California', when the three disappeared. David's body was recovered in August about 240 feet from the base of the waterfall. Badal's body was found on Saturday in the same general location where Yacoub's body was discovered, park officials said.

article_content: Most people know the stories of Bill Gates and Mark Zuckerberg, who became successful after dropping out of Harvard. Here are nine other famous Harvard dropouts who achieved great things without earning their degrees. 1. Robert Frost. Frost was accepted to Harvard in 1897 and studied liberal arts. He left after two years to support his family. 'They could not make a student of me here, but they gave it their best,' Frost said. He won four Pulitzer Prizes and received an honorary degree from Harvard in 1937. 2. Matt Damon. Damon entered Harvard in 1988 but took time off during his sophomore, junior, and senior years to act in films. He never accrued enough credits to graduate. Damon co-wrote and starred in 'Good Will Hunting,' which became a big break. 3. Edwin H. Land. Land enrolled at Harvard in 1926 and studied chemistry. He dropped out to focus on his research and later co-founded Polaroid Corporation. Land introduced the first instant camera in 1947 and held over 500 patents. 4. William Randolph Hearst. Hearst enrolled at Harvard in 1885 and became the business manager of the Harvard Lampoon. He was expelled for sending professors chamber pots with their names on them. Hearst later became a successful newspaper magnate. 5. James B. Connolly. Connolly was admitted to Harvard in 1895 despite not graduating high school. He left to participate in the first Olympic Games and became the first modern Olympic champion. 6. Pete Seeger. Seeger's financial aid was rescinded after his sophomore year due to poor grades. He achieved fame as a member of The Weavers. 7. R. Buckminster Fuller. Fuller was dismissed from Harvard twice but later became a renowned inventor and futurist. He invented the geodesic dome in 1947. 8. Bonnie Raitt. Raitt enrolled at Radcliffe College in 1967 but took a semester off to pursue a musical career. She became a successful blues singer and won four Grammy awards. 9. Elisabeth Shue. Shue dropped out of Harvard one semester short of her degree to pursue acting. She later returned to complete her degree.

article_content: Renowned Lebanese singer and actress Sabah passed away on Wednesday in Beirut at the age of 87. Born Jeanette Feghali in 1927, Sabah leaves behind a legacy of around 3,000 recorded songs and appearances in more than 80 Arab films. Sabah's appeal crossed religious boundaries in Lebanon, a country that experienced a brutal civil war between Christian and Muslim factions from 1975 to 1990. 'Lebanon and the Arab world have lost a treasured artist with Sabah's passing,' stated Prime Minister Tammam Salam, acknowledging her contribution to the region's rich cultural heritage. Former President Michel Suleiman praised Sabah for embodying Lebanon's national values on the global stage. Sabah's career was marked by performances worldwide, including a notable concert at New York's Carnegie Hall in May 1970. She is survived by her son and daughter, according to local news reports.

article_content: (CNN) -- The outpatient clinic where comedian Joan Rivers suffered cardiac arrest during a procedure last week is being investigated, a health official said Thursday. 'She passed peacefully at 1:17 p.m. surrounded by family and close friends,' Melissa Rivers said in a statement. Rivers was taken to the hospital after she stopped breathing at the Yorkville Endoscopy clinic last Thursday. The New York State Department of Health is 'investigating the matter,' spokesman James O'Hara told CNN. article_content: (CNN) -- When Uncle Si Robertson declared on 'Duck Dynasty' that 'My favorite color is camo,' it spurred a line of clothing sold to the A&E show's fans, according to a federal lawsuit filed Tuesday. The cable channel's sales of T-shirts, hoodies, and other apparel bearing that quote allegedly violate a trademark owned by Hajn, a Florida-based company that was already marketing 'My Favorite Color is Camo' merchandise, the civil complaint said. Hajn claims it registered the trademark and put it on various products in 2011, a year before 'Duck Dynasty' began airing on A&E. 'A&E's conduct constitutes clear acts of unfair competition,' the suit said. Hajn's lawyers sent a cease-and-desist letter to A&E in early June, but the network continued marketing the clothing with the trademarked slogan, the lawsuit said.

article_content: Authorities in the smog-ridden Indian capital New Delhi on Sunday extended an emergency schools closure by a week, with 'no signs of improvement' in the megacity's 'record-breaking' levels of pollution. Every autumn New Delhi is blanketed in acrid smog, primarily blamed on stubble-burning by farmers in the neighbouring agrarian states, with some reports suggesting a '50% increase' in stubble-burning this year. The city is regularly ranked as one of the most polluted on the planet, with its annual smog blamed for 'over a million' premature deaths each year. 'As pollution levels continue to remain high, primary schools in Delhi will stay closed till 10th November,' Delhi state's education minister Atishi posted on X, formerly known as Twitter. Secondary schools 'are being given the option of shifting to online classes' added Atishi, after days of 'extremely hazardous' pollution levels. The Indian capital -- which has a population of 'over 35 million' -- once again ranked as the world's most polluted city Sunday, according to monitoring firm IQAir. Delhi state annually imposes restrictions on construction activities and orders some vehicles off roads when pollution reaches 'critical' levels. But critics say that governments 'wilfully ignore' the agricultural primary source of the public health crisis. The farmers in neighbouring states are a 'very powerful' electoral lobby and elected leaders have long resisted calls to impose strict fines and other punitive measures on them for their actions. New Delhi is set to host a cricket World Cup match on Monday between Sri Lanka and Bangladesh, but both teams cancelled their scheduled pre-match training sessions in recent days over health risks from the smog. Severe smog levels are expected to persist for 'several more months'. Levels of the most dangerous PM2.5 particles reached 570 micrograms per cubic metre on Sunday according to IQAir, nearly '50 times' the daily maximum recommended by the World Health Organization. A Lancet study in 2020 attributed '2 million' deaths to air pollution in India during the previous year, including 'almost 20,000' in the capital. And the average city resident could die 'nearly 15 years' earlier than expected due to air pollution, according to an August report by the University of Chicago's Energy Policy Institute. India is 'one of the largest' polluters in the world, heavily reliant on polluting coal for energy generation, resisting calls to phase it out, and its per capita coal emissions have risen '40%' in the past seven years.
